items.title: 52222_Marshall Royal oral history interview
items.q: We were one of the first electrified bands there was, was Lionel Hampton's Orchestra... My brother Ernie and Jack McVea and I, we left the band and went into Lionel's band... I had his band all set out for him

ctx.x: That's the first time -- electric violins weren't even in vogue until 1940. Nobody had any electric anything. There was no electric basses. The first electric basses came out in 1940. We were one of the first electrified bands there was, was Lionel Hampton's Orchestra. We were the innovators of that.
The alto saxophone rather rapidly became your principal instrument, didn't it?

items.title: Lionel Hampton interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, October 18, 1995
items.q: So finally my wife... had got a guy... and then we had Marshall Royal, who was a great saxophone player.

ctx.x: When you had the big band out on the road, it must have been pretty hard to keep so many guys together and happy. Was that a tough job being a leader of a big band.

I tell you, I was always lucky. Because I was always seeking the fine youngsters, you know. They want to be musicians, and was waiting for a break to play in a big band. Because big bands was very popular then, just like when I left Benny Goodman and went out to get my band, there was little kids walking around in California, where I was staying at, after I left Benny Goodman, he took sick. And the doctors who were at the place warned him not to play no more for six months, because he had a disease called…

the clarinet. Well I told him I said “I want you to play tenor.” So finally my wife, my late wife, Gladys, had got a guy and went down to the [sounds like] Lucky Music Company. That’s where all the musicians traded with, and gave him a tenor saxophone, and then we had Marshall Royal, who was a great saxophone player. Marshall, when his brother was coming up, Ernie Royal, Ernie Royal could play really high notes on trumpet.
